1156.title: The Hunter in the Bilva Tree
1156.word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1156.hook: the hunter in the bilva tree can't afford to sleep, and the deer start coming
1156.carry: jagarana: shiva's night is kept awake, together
1156.tomorrow: why say the same five syllables all night?
1156.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri, Hindus who keep the jagarana stay awake through the night, in temples or at home, with bhajans, chanting of Om Namah Shivaya, and rounds of worship of the linga until dawn.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hunter's accidental fast, and upavasa: the fast is staying near Shiva. Today, the long hours after dark, and what kept that hunter awake.
screen: `UPAVASA: STAYING NEAR.` · `NOW, THE LONG NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Back to yesterday's hunter. The Shiva Purana gives him a name, Gurudruha, and a reason to be in that tree: his family is hungry, and he can't go home empty-handed. So he sits on a branch above the pool with his pot of water and his bow, waiting for animals to come and drink. He doesn't sleep; he can't afford to. He has no idea that tonight is the great night of Shiva, or that the stone in the roots below him is a linga. The night is long, and he is about to have visitors.
screen: `A HUNGRY HUNTER.` → `A BRANCH ABOVE THE POOL.` → `HE CAN'T AFFORD TO SLEEP.`

segments.voice: In the first watch of the night, a doe comes down to the water. He draws his bow. And the doe speaks: let me go home first and leave my little ones safe, and i promise i'll come back to you. Hungry as he is, he lets her go. Later another doe comes, then a stag, each with the same plea, each let go on a promise. So the hunter sits on his branch, hour after hour, awake, waiting for deer who may never return. What was happening below him, we'll come to. Today, look at the waking itself. Keeping awake on this night is called jagarana, the vigil, and it's one of the main things Hindus do on Maha Shivaratri. The hunter stayed up for his own reasons, and in the Shiva Purana the night still counted for him. Families who keep it on purpose add two things he didn't have. First, company. In temples the night is cut into four watches, each with its own worship, with bhajans and Om Namah Shivaya in between, so there's always something to wake into. Second, a direction: not just awake, awake toward Shiva. Many teachers read the body's vigil as a rehearsal for the other waking, the one the Katha Upanishad calls for: arise, awake, and learn. If you've ever sat up with family through a long night, at a hospital, a wedding, a wake, you know how it works: nobody keeps the night alone. Shivaratri turns that into worship, and points it at Shiva.
screen: `A DOE: LET ME GO, I'LL COME BACK.` · `JAGARANA: THE VIGIL.` · `FOUR WATCHES, SONGS BETWEEN.` · `AWAKE TOWARD SHIVA.` · then, large: `NOBODY KEEPS THE NIGHT ALONE.`

segments.voice: Sit a little straighter than usual, eyes just slightly open and resting on a spot in front of you, and when the mind starts to drift or dull, the way heads nod at two in the morning, don't scold yourself. Lift: straighten the back, take one fuller breath, and come back, because every lift is a small vigil. If you pray, you can let Om Namah Shivaya, or the name of God you use, be the song that lifts you.
Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva. Today's piece: jagarana, the vigil, kept awake together and pointed toward Shiva, a rehearsal for waking up.

1157.title: Shiva's Tears, the Rudraksha
1157.word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1157.hook: shiva opens his eyes after ages of tapas, his tears become seeds, and the seeds become beads
1157.carry: japa: shiva's name, five syllables, bead by bead
1157.tomorrow: what was falling from the hunter's tree?
1157.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri, some who keep the vigil do japa of Om Namah Shivaya, aloud, whispered or silently, counting on a rudraksha mala, alongside temple songs and worship through the night.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hunter Gurudruha sat awake in a bilva tree: jagarana, Shiva's night is kept awake, together.
screen: `JAGARANA: AWAKE TOGETHER.` · `WHAT FILLS THE HOURS?`

segments.voice: The Shiva Purana tells where these beads come from. Shiva once sat in tapas, deep and still, with his eyes closed, for a thousand years of the gods. When at last he opened his eyes, tears fell. And where they touched the earth, trees grew, with rough brown seeds, wrinkled like tiny walnuts. Those seeds are rudraksha. Tonight, at the temple, a woman sits against a pillar with a string of them in her fingers. Her thumb draws one bead toward her palm, her lips move, and the next bead comes.
screen: `SHIVA OPENS HIS EYES.` → `TEARS BECOME TREES.` → `THE SEEDS BECOME BEADS.`

segments.voice: What moves along those beads is japa: repeating a name of God, again and again. On this night the name is usually Om Namah Shivaya. Namah Shivaya is the Panchakshara, the five-syllable mantra: na, mah, shi, va, ya, salutation to Shiva. You've met it this year, deep inside the Rudram, so the great Vedic hymn and the bead in a tired hand are joined by those five syllables. The Shiva Purana praises this mantra at length. Here's why it suits the night. A long night needs something small. At ten in the evening a long hymn is easy to follow. At three in the morning it slips. Five syllables you can still hold. Japa can be said aloud, whispered, or held silently, so it works in a loud crowd and a quiet room. And the beads do two jobs. They keep count, so the mind doesn't have to. And they give the hand something to do, so when thoughts wander, there's a bead in your fingers, waiting. Now put the story beside it: the beads came from Shiva's tears, and human hands pass them back to him, one name at a time. That's why so many Hindu homes keep a mala near the shrine, and why you'll see a grandparent moving one through their fingers on a bus, in a waiting room, in front of the TV. It's the practice that fits a crowded life: no temple, no hour needed. Just the name, and the next bead.
screen: `RUDRAKSHA: FROM SHIVA'S TEARS.` · `JAPA: THE NAME, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `NAMAH SHIVAYA: FIVE SYLLABLES.` · `SMALL ENOUGH FOR 3 A.M.` · then, large: `THE NAME, AND THE NEXT BEAD.`

segments.voice: Choose something short to repeat, one breath at a time: Om Namah Shivaya if you pray, or a name of God from your own tradition, or simply counting breaths from one to ten. If you have beads, or a string with knots, let the fingers move one at a time, and when you notice you've drifted, don't start over; just take the next bead, the next breath, the next word.
Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva. Today's piece: japa, the name repeated through the night, Om Namah Shivaya on beads the Shiva Purana says grew from his tears.

1158.title: What Fell From the Tree
1158.word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1158.hook: every time the hunter drew his bow, leaves and water fell on a stone he couldn't see
1158.carry: ashutosha: shiva is pleased by a leaf and water
1158.tomorrow: the deer promised to come back. did they?
1158.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri, Hindus bring water, milk, bilva leaves and flowers to Shiva temples and offer them on the linga, sometimes waiting in line through the night; others offer them to a linga or image at home.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shiva's tears became the rudraksha beads, and japa: Shiva's name, five syllables, bead by bead.
screen: `JAPA: THE NAME, AND THE NEXT BEAD.` · `BACK TO THE HUNTER'S TREE.`

segments.voice: Back to the hunter, Gurudruha, up in the bilva tree. Every time a deer came down to the pool, he shifted on his branch and pulled back his bow. And every time he moved, a few bilva leaves shook loose, and water slopped from the pot he'd brought. Down they went in the dark, onto a stone he couldn't see. It was a Shiva linga. Watch after watch, the Shiva Purana says, his fidgeting became worship: water poured, bilva laid down, all night long, by a man who only wanted dinner.
screen: `HE DRAWS HIS BOW.` → `LEAVES AND WATER FALL.` → `ONTO A HIDDEN LINGA.`

segments.voice: This is why the plate looks the way it does on Shivaratri. Go to a Shiva temple that night and look at what people carry: a little pot of water or milk, a few bilva leaves, three to a stem, a flower from the roadside. Nothing that costs much. The water is poured over the linga; the pouring is called abhisheka. Then the bilva, laid on top, the leaf the Shiva Purana praises again and again in his worship. And Shiva has a name for this: Ashutosha, which people explain as the one who is quickly pleased. The hunter's story is how the tradition shows it. He brought no devotion and no gift. A few leaves and a little water, given by accident, and Shiva accepted them. How much more, the story asks, if you give them on purpose? The Bhagavad Gita says something close, in Krishna's voice: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, offered with devotion, is accepted. So the offering isn't a payment, and Shiva isn't a god you have to afford. It's attention put into your hands. You pick the leaf, carry it, wait in line, and set it down with the name on your lips. Then the water runs off, the leaves are cleared away, and nothing is kept. Here's what that means now. You never have to wait until you have enough to come before God. A student with a plastic bottle of water stands in the same line as a family with a silver plate, and for Ashutosha, the water is enough.
screen: `THE HUNTER'S LEAVES FALL.` · `WATER, THEN BILVA.` · `ASHUTOSHA: QUICKLY PLEASED.` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.` · then, large: `YOU NEVER HAVE TO AFFORD HIM.`

segments.voice: Pour a little water into a cup if there's some nearby, or just rest your open hands in your lap, and think of the smallest thing you could give today: a minute of real listening, a kind word you've been holding back. Hold it for a few breaths, then slowly put it down, as if setting a leaf on a stone. If you pray, you can offer it with Shiva's name, or the name of God you use.
Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva. Today's piece: the offering, water and bilva for Ashutosha, the one quickly pleased, given fully and let go.

1159.title: The Deer Come Back at Dawn
1159.word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1159.hook: at first light the deer return to keep their word, and the hunter lowers his bow
1159.carry: parana: the vow ends in giving, then food
1159.tomorrow: how do you know anything is true?
1159.howItsDone: The morning after Maha Shivaratri, those who kept the fast worship again, may give food or gifts, and then break the fast with a simple meal; temples may distribute prasad to the people who kept the night.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hunter's leaves and water fell on a hidden linga, and Ashutosha: Shiva is pleased by a leaf and water. Today the night ends, and so does this part of the path.
screen: `ASHUTOSHA: A LEAF IS ENOUGH.` · `THE NIGHT ENDS.`

segments.voice: The sky over the pool goes from black to gray. The hunter has been awake all night, hungry, and he has let three deer go on their word. Then he hears them. The doe, the second doe, the stag, coming back through the trees together, with their young, just as they promised. Each one steps forward and says: take me first, spare the others. Gurudruha looks at them over his bow. Something in him has changed. He lowers it, and lets them all go.
screen: `BLACK, THEN GRAY.` → `THE DEER COME BACK.` → `HE LOWERS HIS BOW.`

segments.voice: In the Shiva Purana's telling, that's when Shiva appears. The night's worship, the leaves, the water, the waking, has worn away the hunter's hardness. Shiva gives him a new name, Guha, and a promise: one day Rama himself will come to your door. In the Ramayana, Guha is the forest chief who welcomes Rama and ferries him across the Ganga. A hunter who couldn't go home empty-handed became the man who opened his home to God. That's the shape of the morning after Shivaratri, and families still keep it. Breaking a fast at its proper time is called parana. In the Shiva Purana's account of the vow, the night doesn't end with the last song. Morning brings worship again, then giving, and only then is the fast broken. That's why many temples hand out prasad at dawn, and why a grandmother at the gate may give food away before she takes a bite. The vow closes the way the hunter's night closed: the hand that held the bow opens. It closes the Shiva part of the path, too: the pillar no one could measure, Sati and Parvati, Nataraja, a thousand names, the Shiva Sutras, the Rudram, and one great night. And here's what it asks of any big night of prayer, a fast, a festival, a vigil: the test isn't how long you lasted. It's whether the next person you meet gets fed.
screen: `THE DEER COME BACK.` · `GURUDRUHA BECOMES GUHA.` · `PARANA: WORSHIP, GIVING, THEN FOOD.` · `THE SHIVA PART, GATHERED UP.` · then, large: `THE HAND THAT HELD THE BOW OPENS.`

segments.voice: Sit as if the night has just ended and the light is coming up, and walk back slowly through its lessons: the resolve, the fast, the vigil, the name, the offering. Hold the one that stayed with you, and let it go with you into the first ordinary thing you'll do after this sit. If you pray, you can give thanks to Shiva, or to the God you know, for the night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the deer came back at dawn and the hunter lowered his bow: parana, the vow ends in giving, then food. The Shiva part of the path closed with it.
screen: `THE NIGHT ENDS AT DAWN.` · `A NEW PART BEGINS.`

segments.voice: There's a playful old legend about Gautama, the sage tradition credits with the Nyaya Sutra. He was so lost in thought, the story goes, that he walked straight into a well. He climbed out and went right back to thinking. So, the legend says, he was given eyes in his feet, to think and walk at the same time. That's why he's also called Akshapada, eye-footed. It's a joke about philosophers, told with love. And under it sits a real question: when you say you know something, where did that knowing come from?
screen: `LOST IN THOUGHT.` → `INTO THE WELL.` → `HOW DO YOU KNOW ANYTHING?`

segments.voice: This part of the path is the six darshanas. Darshana means seeing, and here a way of seeing: a school of Hindu thought. We'll take them one at a time, side by side, and rank none of them. Nyaya, the school of logic, comes first only because we have to start somewhere. The Nyaya Sutra opens with a list of what it will examine, and the very first is pramana: a means of knowing, a way real knowledge reaches you. It names four. Perception: what you see, hear and touch yourself, like the well in front of your feet. Inference: reasoning from a sign to what you can't see, smoke on a hill, so fire behind it. Comparison: knowing a new thing by its likeness to one you know; the commentators' example is a traveler told that a certain forest animal looks like a cow, who recognizes it when he meets one. And word: the testimony of someone reliable. For Nyaya, that includes the Veda. Here's what surprises people. Scripture isn't set against reason here; it's one of reason's four doors, and the four check each other. And near its start, this book of logic says its aim is release, freedom from suffering. False knowledge leads to faults, faults to action, action to birth, birth to suffering. Remove the false knowledge at the bottom and the whole chain comes loose. So when someone says Hindus just believe things on faith, here's a Hindu school that asked first: how do I know this, and through which door did it come in?
screen: `GAUTAMA, EYE-FOOTED.` · `PRAMANA: A MEANS OF KNOWING.` · `SEE, INFER, COMPARE, BE TOLD.` · `SCRIPTURE: ONE OF FOUR DOORS.` · then, large: `HOW DO I KNOW THIS?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you're sure of today, about a person, about tomorrow, about yourself, and ask quietly where it came from: did you see it, reason to it from a sign, match it to something you knew, or were you told, and by someone how reliable? Don't argue with it; just find its source, and notice whether its sources agree. If you pray, you can ask the God you know for clear sight.
Nyaya. The school of logic, which begins by asking how we know, names four means of knowing, and says the goal of clear thinking is freedom from suffering.

1161.title: The House Built to Burn
1161.hook: Yudhishthira walks into a fine new house, smells ghee and lac, and knows
1161.carry: anumana: a real sign, and a rule that holds
1161.tomorrow: can you prove God exists, step by step?
1161.howItsDone: In traditional Sanskrit study, students of Nyaya learn inference through the example of smoke and fire on a hill, practicing how to state a sign, a rule and a supporting case, and how to spot reasons that only look like reasons.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gautama, the eye-footed sage, and Nyaya: four ways of knowing, aimed at freedom: see, infer, compare, and the word of someone reliable. Today, one of the four, up close.
screen: `NYAYA: FOUR MEANS OF KNOWING.` · `ONE OF THEM, UP CLOSE.`

segments.voice: In the Mahabharata, the five Pandava brothers and their mother are sent off to the town of Varanavata, and lodged in a fine new house. Their cousin Duryodhana had it built. Before they left, their wise uncle Vidura warned Yudhishthira, in a coded riddle, about fire. Now Yudhishthira walks through the door and stops. He smells ghee. He smells fat. He smells lac, the resin that burns fast. He turns to Bhima and says quietly: this house was made to burn.
screen: `A FINE NEW HOUSE.` → `GHEE, FAT, LAC.` → `MADE TO BURN.`

segments.voice: No flame, no confession, and still Yudhishthira knew. Nyaya has a word for that leap: anumana, inference, knowing something you can't see by way of a sign you can. Nyaya teachers lay it out with their classic case: the hill has fire, because it has smoke. It works because smoke and fire have been seen together again and again, at the kitchen hearth; and where there's no fire, like a still lake, there's no smoke. Later Nyaya teachers named that rule vyapti, pervasion: wherever there's smoke, there's fire. With a real sign and a rule that holds, the leap isn't a guess. It's knowing. Yudhishthira's leap had both. The sign was real: he didn't trust a glance; he smelled it, ghee and fat and lac. The rule held: a house made of what burns fastest is made to burn. And a second means of knowing agreed: Vidura's warning, the word of someone reliable. But Nyaya cares just as much how a leap goes wrong. One trap: the sign isn't what you think; a gray haze might be mist, not smoke. Another: the rule run backward. Wherever there's fire, there's smoke? A red-hot iron ball glows with fire and gives off none. And notice, the brothers didn't panic. A digger sent by Vidura made them a tunnel, and on the night the house went up, they slipped away through it. Nyaya doesn't ask you to stop inferring. It asks two questions first, and they work at home too: is the sign real, and does the rule really run this way?
screen: `ANUMANA: FROM A SIGN TO THE UNSEEN.` · `SMOKE ON THE HILL, FIRE BEHIND.` · `HE SMELLED IT, AND VIDURA AGREED.` · `IS IT SMOKE, OR MIST?` · then, large: `IS THE SIGN REAL? DOES THE RULE HOLD?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a conclusion you reached this week about someone from a sign, a look, a silence, a tone of voice, and ask: was it really what I took it for, or could it have been mist? Then ask whether you know this sign always comes with that meaning. Don't decide anything; just let the leap slow down until you can see it, and if you pray, ask the God you know for clear eyes.
Nyaya. Today, anumana, inference: Yudhishthira smelled lac and knew, because the sign was real and the rule held.

1162.howItsDone: In traditional Sanskrit schools, students meet Nyaya through the Nyaya Sutra and its commentaries, learning to set out an argument step by step and to test it in discussion with a teacher.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yudhishthira smelled lac and knew the house was made to burn: anumana, a real sign, and a rule that holds. Today closes a week that began on Shiva's long night.
screen: `ANUMANA: IS THE SIGN REAL?` · `FROM SHIVA'S NIGHT TO NYAYA.`

segments.voice: About a thousand years ago, in Mithila in north India, a Nyaya teacher named Udayana became famous for arguing for God, against sharp critics who said no maker of the world could ever be proved. A story told about him has him arriving at the great Jagannath temple in Puri and finding the doors shut. And Udayana, the story goes, speaks to the Lord, half scolding, half smiling: you ignore me now, but when the doubters came, your case was in my hands.
screen: `A LOGICIAN AT THE TEMPLE.` → `THE DOORS ARE SHUT.` → `YOUR CASE WAS IN MY HANDS.`

segments.voice: His case was built with Nyaya's best-known tool, the argument in five parts. The Nyaya Sutra names them: the proposition, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion. Its early commentator Vatsyayana walks them through with sound: sound does not last, because it is produced; whatever is produced does not last, like a clay pot; sound is produced; so sound does not last. Udayana used that same frame for the biggest question of all. One: the earth and things like it have a maker. Two: because they are effects, put together from parts. Three: whatever is put together has a maker, like a pot and its potter. Four: the earth is put together. Five: so it has a maker, and Nyaya calls that maker Ishvara, the Lord. That's a real Hindu teaching: for Nyaya, God isn't only believed in; God can be reasoned toward. And because every step is said out loud, the other side can test it. Many did. Buddhist thinkers pushed hard on step three: is the world really like a pot? Not every Hindu school agreed either; Mimamsa thinkers saw no need for a maker of the world. Nyaya's answer wasn't to shout louder. It was to lay out the steps, so the disagreement could land where it really lived. So when a friend asks you to prove God, you don't have to choose between a shrug and a fight. You can say: some Hindus tried, in five steps. Here's the step people argue about. What do you think?
screen: `FIVE PARTS, SAID OUT LOUD.` · `SOUND DOESN'T LAST, LIKE A POT.` · `THE WORLD HAS A MAKER, LIKE A POT.` · `CRITICS TESTED STEP THREE.` · then, large: `REASON TOWARD GOD, OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: Listen to one sound, a chime if you have one, or whatever comes next, and follow it all the way down into quiet. Then hold up one rule of thumb you live by, like anyone who's late doesn't care, and look for its pot: one real case where it plainly held, and one where it didn't. If you pray, you can rest in the name of God you use as the silence settles.
Nyaya. The school of logic, and its argument in five parts, which Udayana used to reason toward Ishvara, the Lord.
screen: `NYAYA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Nyaya reasons toward God, step by step, out loud. A good reason can point to its pot. I'll be here tomorrow.
